tagline: Paul's longest and most carefully argued letter: the gospel of God's righteousness, for Jew and Gentile alike, set out for a church he had never visited.
overview:
Romans is a letter, but it reads at times like a sustained argument. Paul wrote it to the Christians in Rome, a mixed community of Jewish and Gentile believers whom he had not yet met, to introduce himself and the gospel he preached before he arrived. He states his theme early: the gospel “is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, first to the Jew, then to the Greek” (1:16), because in it “the righteousness of God” is revealed (1:17). The rest of the letter works that sentence out.

The argument moves in large blocks. Paul first shows that the whole human race, Gentile and Jew, stands guilty before God (1:18-3:20). He then announces that God has acted in Jesus Christ to put people right with himself as a gift received by faith, and shows that Abraham was counted righteous in exactly that way (3:21-4:25). He describes the new life that follows: peace with God, freedom from the reign of sin and death, the struggle with the law, and life in the Spirit that ends in the renewal of all creation (chapters 5 to 8). He wrestles openly with the painful question of why most of his own people, Israel, have not believed (chapters 9 to 11). Finally he turns to how a people saved by mercy should live together, especially when Jewish and Gentile believers disagree over food and holy days (12:1-15:13), and closes with his travel plans and a long list of greetings.

Few books have shaped Christian history as much. Romans stands behind turning points in the lives of Augustine, Martin Luther, and John Wesley, and behind the Protestant Reformation's teaching on justification by faith. It remains at the center of debate today about what Paul meant by the law, by works, and by righteousness. A first-time reader will find it demanding, but its questions are the deepest ones: what is wrong with us, what God has done about it, and what kind of people that makes us.
author:
The letter names Paul as its author (1:1), and this is one of the few points in New Testament scholarship on which virtually everyone agrees. Romans belongs with Galatians and the Corinthian letters as the core of the undisputed Pauline letters, and even the most skeptical critical traditions have accepted it as his. Paul dictated it: a man named Tertius, who actually wrote it down, adds his own greeting near the end (16:22), which was common practice for letters in the Roman world.

The debates concern the letter's form rather than its author. Early manuscripts show that Romans circulated in more than one form, and the closing doxology (16:25-27) appears at different places in different manuscripts. Some scholars have argued that chapter 16, with its many greetings to named people, was originally a separate note sent to Ephesus, since Paul seems to know a surprising number of people in a city he had never visited. Most scholars today hold that chapter 16 belongs to the letter to Rome, noting that travel between Rome and the eastern cities was frequent and that Paul had good reason to greet every acquaintance he had in a church where he hoped to be welcomed.
date: Romans is usually dated to about AD 57, with a range of roughly AD 55 to 58, and it was most likely written from Corinth in Greece. The evidence fits together well. Paul says he is about to take a collection from the churches of Macedonia and Achaia to the poor believers in Jerusalem (15:25-26), which matches the end of his third missionary campaign. Acts reports that he then spent three months in Greece before that trip to Jerusalem (Acts 20:2-3). The letter commends Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae, the eastern port of Corinth, who probably carried it (16:1-2), and it sends greetings from Gaius, Paul's host (16:23), likely the Gaius Paul baptized in Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:14). The exact year depends on how one reconstructs Paul's chronology, but the setting is widely agreed.
setting:
Rome in the 50s AD was the capital of an empire that ran from Spain to Syria, a crowded city of perhaps a million people drawn from every province. It had a large Jewish community, with many synagogues, and the gospel almost certainly reached Rome through Jewish believers who had traveled there, well before any apostle arrived. Nobody knows who first founded the church; Paul himself never claims it, and he says he has not yet visited (1:13).

An event under the emperor Claudius shaped the church Paul addressed. The Roman historian Suetonius reports that Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome because of constant disturbances at the instigation of one Chrestus, which many scholars take as a garbled reference to disputes about Christ. Acts mentions the same expulsion: Aquila and Priscilla had come to Corinth from Italy because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome (Acts 18:2). The edict is usually dated to about AD 49, though some date it earlier. For several years the Roman church would have been led largely by Gentile believers. After Claudius died in AD 54, Jews were able to return (Priscilla and Aquila are back in Rome in Romans 16:3), and a church that had grown in a Gentile direction now had to welcome back Jewish believers with their own convictions about food, the Sabbath, and the law. Many interpreters read the letter's concern for Jew and Gentile together, and its long appeal for mutual acceptance in chapters 14 and 15, against that background.
purpose:
Paul gives some of his reasons himself. He had long wanted to visit Rome (1:10-15). He was about to go to Jerusalem with the collection, and he was anxious about how he would be received there (15:30-31). After that he planned to go on to Spain and hoped the Roman church would help send him (15:24, 28). The letter introduces him and his gospel to a church whose support he needed, and it answers suspicions that his preaching of grace made the law worthless or encouraged sin (3:8, 6:1).

Beyond those practical aims, scholars weigh how much of the letter addresses tensions inside the Roman church itself. Some read Romans chiefly as a summary of Paul's gospel, prepared at a turning point in his work. Others stress that its long treatment of Jew and Gentile, of Israel's future, and of the strong and the weak addresses a divided congregation that needed to hear that God's mercy had made them one people. Most see both aims at work.
story: Romans comes after the Gospels and Acts in the Christian Bible and opens the collection of Paul's letters. Historically it belongs inside the story of Acts: Paul wrote it during the three months in Greece described in Acts 20:2-3, just before the trip to Jerusalem where he was arrested (Acts 21). When Acts closes with Paul finally in Rome, under guard, the church there already has this letter in its hands. Romans also looks back across the whole Old Testament, drawing on Genesis, the Psalms, Isaiah, and the prophets more heavily than any other Pauline letter, to argue that the gospel is not a new religion but the fulfillment of what God promised Abraham and spoke through the prophets.
christ: Romans opens by defining the gospel as the message about God's Son, descended from David according to the flesh and declared Son of God with power by his resurrection from the dead (1:3-4). Everything in the letter hangs on that person and what he has done. Christ's death is the place where God displays his righteousness and deals with sin (3:21-26). He is the second Adam, whose obedience undoes the ruin that came through the first (5:12-21). Believers are united with him in his death and resurrection (chapter 6), are free from condemnation because they are in him (8:1), and share his inheritance as God's children (8:17). He is the goal of the law (10:4), the one Israel's Scriptures promised, and the Lord whom Jew and Gentile call on alike (10:12-13). Romans is not a treatise on salvation in the abstract. It is a letter about what God has done in Jesus.
reading:
Read Romans as an argument, and follow the conversation. Paul often raises an objection in the voice of an imagined opponent and answers it, a style ancient teachers called the diatribe, so a question such as “What then shall we say?” usually signals a turn. Read whole sections before stopping on single verses, since many famous verses mean more inside their paragraph than on a poster. Notice how often Paul quotes the Old Testament and pay attention to the passages he quotes.

Two common misreadings are worth avoiding. The first treats Romans as only about how an individual gets to heaven, missing its concern for how Jews and Gentiles become one people under God. The second swings the other way and treats it only as a letter about ethnic groups, missing its searching treatment of sin, guilt, and grace for every person. The letter holds both together. It also rewards patience: chapters 9 to 11 are not a detour but the place where Paul asks whether God has kept his promises, which is the question the whole letter depends on.

structure.title: Greeting and theme
structure.summary: Paul introduces himself, his gospel about God's Son, and his long-delayed plan to visit Rome, then states the letter's theme: the gospel is God's power for salvation, revealing his righteousness by faith.

structure.title: The whole world under sin
structure.summary: Gentiles who suppressed what they knew of God, and Jews who had the law and did not keep it, stand together before God's judgment. No one is declared righteous by works of the law.

structure.title: Righteousness through faith
structure.summary: God has revealed his righteousness apart from the law through faith in Jesus Christ (or, as some read the Greek, the faithfulness of Jesus Christ), whose death is the place of atonement. Abraham, counted righteous by faith before circumcision, is the father of all who believe.

structure.title: New life and sure hope
structure.summary: Justified believers have peace with God. Christ undoes Adam's ruin, believers die and rise with him, the law's role is explored, and life in the Spirit ends in the hope that nothing can separate them from God's love.

structure.title: God's faithfulness and Israel
structure.summary: Paul grieves Israel's unbelief and argues that God's word has not failed. God's mercy is free, a remnant believes, Gentiles are grafted in, and all Israel will be saved.

structure.title: The life of a people shaped by mercy
structure.summary: Believers offer themselves to God, serve one another with their gifts, love their enemies, live under the governing authorities, and welcome one another across disputes about food and days.

structure.title: Paul's plans and greetings
structure.summary: Paul explains his mission, his coming trip to Jerusalem with the collection, and his hope to reach Spain, then greets many believers in Rome by name and closes with praise to God.

themes.title: The righteousness of God
themes.body: Paul's theme phrase has been read in several ways: as the righteous standing God gives to believers, as God's own saving faithfulness to his promises, or as both at once. The letter shows God as just in judging sin and just in justifying the one who believes (3:26). Whatever the precise emphasis, the phrase names God acting in Christ to set things right.

themes.title: Sin and death as powers
themes.body: Romans treats sin not only as wrong acts but as a power that reigns over humanity, entering through Adam and bringing death with it. That is why the answer cannot be simple self-improvement. People need to be rescued and brought under a new reign, the reign of grace.

themes.title: Faith and the law
themes.body: Paul insists that no one is justified by works of the law, yet he calls the law holy, righteous, and good. Faith does not nullify the law but upholds it. How to hold these together is one of the letter's great questions, and the key to much of the modern debate about Paul.

themes.title: Jew and Gentile together
themes.body: The gospel is for the Jew first and also for the Greek. God is not the God of Jews only, Abraham is the father of all who believe, and the church must welcome one another as Christ welcomed them. The unity of one people from many nations runs through the letter from its first chapter to its last.

themes.title: The Spirit and hope
themes.body: The Spirit gives life, bears witness that believers are God's children, helps them in weakness, and is the firstfruits of a coming redemption that will reach the whole groaning creation. Romans holds present suffering and future glory together.

keyChapters.why: The letter's theme (1:16-17) and its opening account of humanity's refusal to honor God.
The verdict that all have sinned, and the central statement of righteousness through faith and Christ's atoning death (3:21-26).
Abraham as the pattern of justification by faith and the father of Jewish and Gentile believers alike.
Peace with God, and the comparison of Adam and Christ that frames the human story.
Union with Christ in his death and resurrection, and freedom from the reign of sin.
Life in the Spirit, adoption, the hope of creation, and the assurance that nothing can separate believers from God's love.
The start of Paul's wrestling with Israel's unbelief and God's freedom in mercy.
The turn to the life of a people shaped by mercy, beginning with bodies offered as living sacrifices.
